title: What Does 1 Over 1, 2 Over 1 and 2 Over 2 Mean in Cross Stitch?

seo.title: What Does 1 Over 1, 2 Over 1 and 2 Over 2 Mean in Cross Stitch?
seo.meta_description: Learn what 1 over 1, 2 over 1 and 2 over 2 mean in cross stitch, how thread strands and fabric threads are counted, and when each setup changes size and coverage.
seo.search_intent: Explain cross stitch over-one and over-two notation clearly, including strand count, fabric-thread count, finished size, coverage and when each setup is used.

excerpt: A clear guide to 1 over 1, 2 over 1 and 2 over 2 notation, including strands, fabric threads, finished size, coverage and common mistakes.
content_html:
Cross stitch instructions sometimes use shorthand such as “2 over 2” or “1 over 1”, especially when the project is stitched on linen or evenweave. The notation can look technical, but it describes two separate choices: how many strands of embroidery floss are in the needle and how many fabric threads each full cross covers. Once those two parts are separated, the system is much easier to read.

What the two numbers actually mean

In the phrase “2 over 2”, the first number normally means two strands of floss are used together in the needle. The second number means each cross is worked over two fabric threads horizontally and vertically. “1 over 1” therefore means one strand of floss over one fabric thread, while “2 over 1” means two strands of floss over one fabric thread. This notation is most useful on evenweave and linen because their structure allows stitches to be placed over one thread or over several threads.

The expression does not describe the number of individual legs in the cross. A normal cross stitch still has two diagonal legs. It also does not mean “two stitches over two squares” in the way an Aida chart is usually read. The numbers refer to floss strands and fabric threads, not to chart symbols.

Why over two is common on linen and evenweave

When stitching over two fabric threads, the needle travels from one intersection to the intersection two threads away. This creates a larger visual square and makes the fabric behave more like Aida, where one visible block normally corresponds to one chart square. On 28-count evenweave stitched over two, the effective stitch density is about 14 stitches per inch. On 32-count fabric over two, it is about 16 stitches per inch.

This is why a pattern designed for 14-count Aida can often be stitched at approximately the same finished size on 28-count evenweave over two. The underlying fabric count is different, but each cross spans two threads, which halves the effective stitch count per inch. The same logic works for 16-count Aida and 32-count evenweave over two.

What changes when you stitch over one

Over-one stitching uses every fabric-thread intersection, so the finished stitches are much smaller. A design stitched one over one on 28-count evenweave is roughly twice as dense in each direction as the same chart stitched over two. That means the finished width and height are roughly halved if the chart dimensions remain unchanged.

Because the crosses are smaller, over-one work can hold fine detail and is useful for miniature motifs, detailed faces or small lettering. It also demands more careful counting because each fabric thread matters. On loosely woven linen, a stitch can occasionally slip around the fabric thread if the tension is too firm, so many stitchers prefer a gentler pull or a suitable starting position for the first leg.

How strand count affects coverage

The first number controls how much floss fills the stitch. Two strands usually give fuller coverage than one, but the best choice depends on fabric count, thread type, color contrast and personal preference. Dark floss on pale fabric can show gaps differently from pale floss on pale fabric, and higher-count fabrics generally need less thread bulk than lower-count fabrics.

“2 over 2” is therefore not automatically better than “1 over 2”, and “2 over 1” is not always appropriate just because two strands are common on Aida. On high-count fabric, two strands over one may feel crowded and make the holes difficult to use. A small test patch is more reliable than assuming one strand formula suits every fabric.

How the notation affects finished size

Finished size depends on the number of chart stitches and the effective stitches per inch. If a chart is 140 stitches wide and is worked over two on 28-count fabric, the effective count is about 14 stitches per inch, producing a stitched width of about 10 inches. If the same chart is worked over one on the same 28-count fabric, the effective count is 28 stitches per inch, so the stitched width is about 5 inches.

This distinction matters when buying fabric, choosing a hoop or frame and deciding whether small details will remain readable. Before changing from over two to over one, recalculate the finished dimensions rather than assuming the pattern will simply look “finer”. The entire physical scale of the design changes.

Common mistakes when reading over-one and over-two instructions

One common mistake is confusing strand count with fabric count. “Two over two” does not mean 22-count fabric, and it does not indicate needle size. Another is counting visible holes rather than fabric threads, especially on linen where the weave can be less visually regular than Aida. Count the threads or intersections carefully until the rhythm becomes familiar.

It is also easy to change one part of the formula and forget the other. If a designer recommends two strands over two and you decide to stitch over one, you may also need to reconsider the number of strands because the stitch is now much smaller. Make a short sample if coverage is uncertain.

For practical use, read the notation from left to right as “strands over fabric threads”. Then check the fabric count and calculate the effective stitch density before cutting fabric. That simple sequence prevents most sizing and coverage errors and makes linen and evenweave instructions much less intimidating.
